post.title: How to write strong work experience in your resume
post.subtitle: A clean structure for describing impact, responsibility, and growth so recruiters can scan and understand your value quickly.
post.author: Andrew Scott

why.title: Why work experience matters
why.paragraph1: When recruiters scan resumes, their eyes often land on the work experience section first. It is your chance to prove how past roles prepared you for the next opportunity.
why.paragraph2: A strong experience section does not just list duties. It tells a short story of impact: what problem you worked on, what actions you took, and what changed because of your work.

strengthen.title: Tips to strengthen your work experience
strengthen.paragraph1: Instead of writing a generic responsibility, describe what changed because of your contribution. Numbers, time savings, conversion impact, or process improvements help reviewers evaluate your experience faster.
strengthen.bullet2: Start bullets with action verbs (built, improved, launched, reduced, automated).
strengthen.bullet4: Keep examples relevant to the target role.
strengthen.bullet5: Show growth over time (scope, ownership, leadership).

rewrite.title: Example rewrite
rewrite.paragraph1: Weak: "Responsible for managing a sales team."
rewrite.paragraph2: Stronger: "Led a team of 6 sales reps, introduced a weekly pipeline review, and increased close rate by 18% over two quarters."
rewrite.paragraph3: The second version gives scope, action, and outcome. That combination is what makes resume bullets memorable.

takeaway.title: Final takeaway
takeaway.paragraph1: Your work experience section should help a recruiter answer one question quickly: can this person create results in a similar environment here?
takeaway.paragraph2: Write for clarity first, then tighten wording. Short, concrete bullets outperform long generic descriptions almost every time.
